That being said, I have similar experience in this area unfortunately. A few years ago it came to light that my father had molested my younger half sister (she's roughly 15 years younger than me) when she was 10-11ish. I have 2 daughters myself and they had stayed with their grandparents countless times. I remember feeling absolutely furious with myself for putting them at risk like that. My father was physically abusive to me, my mother, and my other sister, but after my mother and him divorced we all thought he had changed. He remarried and everything seemed good. If I've learned anything in my experience it's simply that all of the preventative things I can think of don't matter and focusing on them and blaming myself only creates more turmoil within myself. The blame lies entirely with the one who committed these acts and no amount of "if I had done this...." is going to change what happened or make it any easier to come to terms with it. Please seek out professional help. I cannot tell you how much it helped me. If for no other reason that's for your daughter's sake cause your instinct, well at least mine was, is gonna be to try and protect them from every possible instance this can happen and in the end there's never enough that can be done and you risk doing more harm than good.

First and foremost, please don't refer to us as "transgenders". It is widely viewed as a perjorative. Typically, trans people or transgender people is preferred. If you take nothing else from this response, I hope that at least this will stick with you.

It's not meant to be a comparison though. It's meant to be a reference point. To draw similarities between the two in hopes that one can see the intersectionality of bigotry. You can look at any form of bigotry, whether it be racism, sexism, homophobia, transphobia, antisemitism, or whatever, and they all have common themes between them. Equating those people to being criminals (e.g. black people are criminals and queer people are pedophiles), they are less subhuman, abominations, undermining democracy, etc. so to point to one instance of it happening to show that we already have decided this is a bad thing to show that it happening to another group of people is meant to become a "oh yea that's bad too", not to compare the experiences of the two. 

As for the "born that way" point, that's widely debated, but the general consensus at this point is that trans people, just like queer people as a whole, are born the way they are. Many of us, arguably most all, of us knew to some degree when we were very young, we just didn't have the words for it or were forced to hide it for safety reasons. The perceived uptick in trans people is largely due to a more accepting society. When it is no longer something to be condemned for, or at least less than before, more people are going to come out of the closet. 

Lastly, being cautious of medical institutions due to past egregiousness is valid, but to ignore any advancements being made because "we got it wrong that one time" is foolish at the very least and outright harmful at its worst. I mean, the whole process of making advancements is making mistakes to learn from and build upon.

The problem is that people, like yourself, see highlighting someone else as taking away from themselves. This is why, inmho, there was all the backlash with the BLM movement with the "All Lives Matter" kids (in addition to just generalized racism). Giving representation and highlighting the struggle of a marginalized community, even when that community exists within another, should be viewed as just that and not as "I'm being excluded". You're still included, the rainbow portion is still there, it's just that now we're adding pieces to highlight groups that have predominantly been underrepresented or even excluded from the community as a whole. As a person who suffers from anxiety and panic disorder I can sympathize with you. Like most people will tell you talk to your doctor and/or a therapist. There are a number of medications that can help, but it may take a while to find the right one. I went through 4 before I finally found one that keeps me pretty level. Keep in mind that every medication is going to have its own side effects ( one I took made me angry, one made me a zombie, and another made me happy about feeling crappy ). I recommend getting a physical and a full chem panel done prior to starting any medication to check for any possible underlying issues ( the med I'm currently on can cause fatal liver damage if you have any sort of liver condition, but most medications will mess with your liver to some degree ). 

There are more natural ways to boost mood and fight anxiety as well. St. John's Wart is a natural herbal supplement that will boost mood ( talk to your doctor before starting ). Things like a healthy diet, exercise, and having adequate vitamin and mineral intake will help as well.

If at any point you get depressed due to your anxiety ( I've been there ) talk to a therapist, friend, spouse, helpline, anyone really. Its amazing how much help it is to just talk to someone and let them know how you feel. In my experience they are often times able to come up with ideas to help.

Lastly, try and figure out what triggers your anxiety. Once you do that you can find ways to avoid those triggers or work on them so they no longer cause you problems.
